entry: Colonial war in [[French Indochina]] between the French Union and the Viet Minh, fought mostly in Vietnam. [[Ho Chi Minh]] proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam on September 2, 1945, and French forces overthrew the Viet Minh administration in Saigon on September 23. Full-scale war broke out in December 1946, after a year of low-level fighting and failed negotiations. The [[United States]] aided France, while [[China]] and the [[Soviet Union]] backed the Viet Minh. After a decisive French defeat at Dien Bien Phu, the Viet Minh accepted, under Chinese diplomatic pressure, a separation at the 17th parallel. The war ended on August 11, 1954. An estimated 400,000 to 842,707 soldiers died, along with between 125,000 and 400,000 civilians. Both sides committed [[War crime|war crimes]], including killings of civilians, rape and torture.

Conflict (1839–1842) between the [[British Empire]] and [[Qing dynasty|Qing China]], triggered by Chinese enforcement of a ban on the [[Opium|opium]] trade. Qing officials seized opium stocks, mainly from British merchants at [[Guangzhou]] (then named Canton). After British dealers handed over 1,420 tonnes (3.1 million lb) of opium in March 1839, Viceroy Lin Zexu had it destroyed publicly on June 3, 1839. After British sailors killed a Chinese villager that July, the [[Royal Navy]] won a series of decisive victories. British forces occupied [[Hong Kong]] in January 1841. The Treaty of Nanking, imposed on August 29, 1842, granted an indemnity and extraterritoriality to British subjects, opened five treaty ports and ceded Hong Kong Island in perpetuity. Many historians regard 1839 as the beginning of modern Chinese history. The social unrest that followed formed a background to the [[Taiping Rebellion]].

War (1894–1895) between the [[Qing dynasty|Qing dynasty of China]] and the [[Empire of Japan]], fought mainly for influence over [[Korea]]. Japanese land and naval forces made sustained gains, and the Beiyang Fleet suffered a decisive defeat at the Battle of the Yalu River. Japan captured Lüshunkou (Port Arthur) on November 21, 1894, and Weihaiwei on February 12, 1895. The Qing sued for peace, and the Treaty of Shimonoseki, signed April 17, 1895, required a massive indemnity and the cession of [[Taiwan]] to Japan. Japan also gained a predominant position in Korea. The war exposed the failure of Qing efforts to modernize its military, in contrast with Japan's [[Meiji Restoration]]. For the first time, regional dominance in East Asia shifted from China to Japan. The defeat fueled upheaval led by [[Sun Yat-sen]] and Kang Youwei, culminating in the [[1911 Revolution]] and the end of dynastic rule in China.

Immediate care for a person in a medical emergency, given to preserve life, prevent worsening or promote recovery until medical services arrive. It is generally performed by someone with basic medical or first-response training. Mental health first aid extends the concept to mental health. Five general steps are assessing the surroundings, moving to safety, calling for help, performing suitable first aid for the [[Injury|injury]] and evaluating the casualty. Bandaging of battle [[Wound|wounds]] appears on Classical Greek pottery from c. 500 BC. [[Napoleon|Napoleon's]] surgeon, Baron Dominique-Jean Larrey, created an ambulance corps tasked with first aid in battle. After Swiss businessman Jean-Henri Dunant witnessed the aftermath of the Battle of Solferino in 1859, his work led to the formation of the Red Cross, which with the Red Crescent remains the largest provider of first aid worldwide. In 1870, Prussian surgeon Friedrich von Esmarch introduced formalized first aid to the military, including training for soldiers in the [[Franco-Prussian War]].

Law of thermodynamics applying [[Conservation of energy|conservation of energy]] to thermodynamic processes. Energy cannot be created or destroyed, but it can be transformed from one form to another, and the sum of all forms of energy in an isolated system is constant. For a system without transfer of matter, the law distinguishes energy transferred as [[Heat|heat]] and as [[Work (physics)|work]], and defines the [[Internal energy|internal energy]] of the system. The change in internal energy equals the heat supplied minus the work done by the system (ΔU = Q − W). The law makes perpetual motion machines of the first kind impossible.

Formal system, also called predicate logic or predicate calculus, that uses quantified variables over non-logical objects. Unlike [[Propositional logic|propositional logic]], it allows statements such as: for all x, if x is a human, then x is mortal. The term distinguishes it from higher-order logic, in which predicates can take predicates or functions as arguments. Its foundations were developed independently by [[Gottlob Frege]] and [[Charles Sanders Peirce]] in the 1880s. Many sound and complete deductive systems exist for it, and it is the standard for formalizing [[Mathematics|mathematics]] into axioms. [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]] and Peano arithmetic are first-order axiomatizations of set theory and [[Number theory|number theory]]. No first-order theory, however, can uniquely describe a structure with an infinite domain, such as the natural numbers or the real line.

Fish caught and eaten by humans in virtually all regions of the world. Fish meat has been an important dietary source of [[Protein (nutrient)|protein]] and other nutrients. Since 1961, apparent global food fish consumption has risen by an average of 3.2 percent a year, outpacing population growth of 1.6 percent. Per capita consumption grew from 9.0 kg (19.8 lb) in 1961 to 20.2 kg (45 lb) in 2015. In 2015, [[Asia]] consumed more than two-thirds of the world total of 149 million tonnes. Over 32,000 fish species have been described, but only about 20 percent are used by humans as food. Fish may be served raw, cured by marinating, [[Pickling|pickling]] or [[Smoking (cooking)|smoking]], or cooked by baking, frying, [[Grilling|grilling]], poaching or [[Steaming|steaming]]. A 150 g portion provides about 50 to 60 percent of an adult's daily protein requirement.

Economic branch that takes, cultures, processes, preserves, transports, markets or sells fish and fish products. Also called the seafood industry, its products include non-food items such as [[Pearl|pearls]]. The Food and Agriculture Organization includes recreational, subsistence and commercial fishing, along with related harvesting, processing and marketing. The livelihoods of over 500 million people in developing countries depend directly or indirectly on fisheries and [[Aquaculture|aquaculture]]. The world harvest stabilized around 85–95 million metric tons a year by 1986. In 2005, commercial wild fisheries captured 93.3 million metric tons, and fish farms produced 48.1 million metric tons. Stocks fished within biologically sustainable levels fell from 90% in 1974 to 62.3% in 2021. Overfishing, [[Climate change|climate change]] and biodiversity loss threaten the livelihoods and food security of a substantial part of the global population.

Boat or ship used to catch fish and other aquatic animals such as [[Shrimp|shrimp]] and krill at sea, on lakes or on rivers. Before the 1950s, fishing boats were little standardized, and traditional ones were built of [[Wood|wood]]. Fiberglass is increasingly used for vessels up to 25 meters, and [[Steel|steel]] for larger ones. The oldest boats found by archaeologists are dugout canoes from the [[Neolithic]] period, 7,000–9,000 years old. The Khufu ship, a 143-foot (44 m) vessel entombed at the foot of the [[Great Pyramid of Giza]] around 2,500 BC, shows the skill of Egyptian shipbuilders. Scandinavian builders incorporated iron into their designs and developed oars for propulsion, innovations that influenced fishing boat design long after the Viking period. In the 15th century, the Dutch developed a seagoing [[Herring|herring]] drifter that became a blueprint for European fishing vessels. Recreational fishing boats range from dinghies to superyachts.

Division of a single entity, usually a [[Cell (biology)|cell]], into two or more parts that each regenerate into a separate entity resembling the original. In binary fission, one entity produces two parts. It is a form of [[Asexual reproduction|asexual reproduction]] used by [[Archaea]] and [[Bacteria]] and by some organelles, such as [[Mitochondria|mitochondria]]. The single DNA molecule replicates, and each copy attaches to a different part of the cell membrane, so the daughter cells are genetically identical barring random [[Mutation|mutations]]. Unlike [[Mitosis|mitosis]], binary fission forms no spindle apparatus. In bacteria, FtsZ, homologous to β-tubulin, assembles into a Z ring that defines the division plane. *E. coli* cells typically divide about every 20 minutes at 37 °C. Multiple fission, by contrast, produces more than two parts.

headword: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period
sort_key: five dynasties and ten kingdoms period
entry: Era of political fragmentation in imperial [[China]], 907–979. Five dynastic states succeeded one another in the Central Plain, while more than a dozen concurrent states were established elsewhere, mainly in South China; the most powerful ten were known as the ten kingdoms. The era is traditionally dated from the fall of the [[Tang dynasty]] in 907 to the founding of the [[Song dynasty]] in 960. Song then spent 19 years subduing the remaining southern states, and the last Five Dynasties regime, Northern Han, fell to Song in 979. The [[Liao dynasty]] remained in the north until it was succeeded by the [[Jin dynasty (1115–1234)|Jin dynasty]]. Southern kingdoms were comparatively stable, which enabled trade, land reclamation and infrastructure projects that laid the groundwork for the Song economic boom.

Five obligatory acts of worship for all Muslims, forming the foundation of Islamic religious practice. They are the shahada (profession of faith), salah (prayer), zakat (almsgiving), sawm (fasting during [[Ramadan]]) and [[Hajj|hajj]] (pilgrimage to [[Mecca]]). The shahada affirms that there is no god but God and that [[Muhammad]] is the messenger of God. Each pillar is alluded to in the [[Quran]], and the [[Hadith]] gives further detail. The practices are particularly emphasized in [[Sunni Islam]], and Shia Muslims also recognize them as fundamental, although their classification may differ. Individual observance varies, and some communities, such as the Alevis, reject the pillars and follow a Four Doors system instead.

Heavier-than-air [[Aircraft|aircraft]] that generates [[Lift (force)|lift]] from fixed wings, distinct from rotary-wing aircraft and ornithopters. Gliding aircraft, including free-flying [[Glider (aircraft)|gliders]] and tethered [[Kite|kites]], use moving air to gain altitude, while powered airplanes gain forward thrust from an engine. Most are operated by a pilot, but some are remotely controlled or fully autonomous. Kites were used in China about 2,800 years ago, and paper kites were flying by 549 AD. In 1799, Sir George Cayley laid out the concept of the modern airplane as a fixed-wing machine with systems for lift, propulsion and control, and in 1853 he built a successful passenger-carrying glider. The [[Wright brothers]]' flights in 1903 with the [[Wright Flyer]] are recognized by the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale as the first sustained and controlled heavier-than-air powered flight.

Long, relatively narrow sea inlet with steep sides or cliffs, in a valley created by a former [[Glacier|glacier]] and since flooded by the sea. Fjords are the glacial equivalent of drowned river valleys, known as rias. They occur on the coasts of [[Antarctica]], the [[Arctic]] and surrounding landmasses. A glacier forms a fjord by cutting a U-shaped valley, which the sea later floods. Most fjords are deeper than the adjacent sea; Sognefjord, in [[Norway]], reaches as much as 1,300 m (4,265 ft) below sea level. Many have a sill or shoal at the mouth, which can create extreme currents. Norway's coastline is estimated at 29,000 km (18,000 mi) including its nearly 1,200 fjords, but only 2,500 km (1,600 mi) when the fjords are excluded.

Piece of fabric, most often rectangular, with a distinctive design, flown from a pole for symbolic, signaling or decorative purposes. The study of flags is called vexillology, from the Latin *vexillum*, meaning flag or banner. The first flags aided military coordination on battlefields, and they later became a common tool for signaling and identification. The origin of the flag is unknown, but the oldest flag discovered is a bronze example from Shahdad, Iran, dating to c. 2400 BC. Cloth flags were almost certainly invented either in the Indian subcontinent or by the [[Zhou dynasty]] of ancient China. European flags developed independently, and the Roman cloth flag known as the *vexillum* is described as the root of the modern European flag tradition. In medieval Europe, flags developed in connection with warfare, Christianity, [[Heraldry|heraldry]] and [[Monarchy|monarchy]]. Modern [[National flag|national flags]] are associated with state formation, citizenship, revolution and [[Nationalism|nationalism]] after 1789.

National flag, a blue disc with a starry sky, spanned by a curved band reading *Ordem e Progresso*, within a yellow rhombus on a green field. Adopted on November 19, 1889, four days after the Proclamation of the Republic, it replaced the flag of the [[Empire of Brazil]]. The green field and yellow rhombus were kept from the imperial flag, where they stood for the House of Braganza and the [[House of Habsburg]]. The motto derives from the [[Positivism|positivist]] motto of [[Auguste Comte]]. Each of the 27 stars represents a federal unit; the flag gained stars in 1960, 1968 and 1992.

National flag, popularly called the Maple Leaf, with a white square centered between red bands in a 1:2:1 ratio and a red 11-pointed maple leaf. It was the first flag adopted by both houses of Parliament and officially proclaimed by the Canadian monarch. A committee formed by Prime Minister Lester B. Pearson in 1964 selected George Stanley's maple leaf design from three choices. The flag first appeared on February 15, 1965, a date now celebrated as National Flag of Canada Day. The [[Union Jack]] remains an official flag, symbolizing allegiance to the monarch and membership in the [[Commonwealth of Nations]].

Red national flag of the People's Republic of China, with five golden stars in the canton. Officially, red stands for the Chinese Communist Revolution, the large star for the [[Chinese Communist Party]] and the four smaller stars for the people. Adopted upon the proclamation of the People's Republic on October 1, 1949, the flag was designed by Zeng Liansong and first hoisted by the [[People's Liberation Army]] over [[Tiananmen Square]]. The original design linked the four small stars to the four social classes in [[Mao Zedong]]'s theory of New Democracy. The 1992 National Flag Law describes the stars only as symbols of the People's Republic.

National flag, a tricolor of vertical blue, white and red bands, adopted during the [[French Revolution]]. The Paris militia wore a blue and red cockade. According to [[Marquis de Lafayette|Lafayette]], white, the ancient French color, was added to form a tricolor cockade, which became the basis of the flag adopted in 1790. A modified design by [[Jacques-Louis David]] followed in 1794. The tricolor returned after the [[July Revolution]] of 1830. A lighter blue version was introduced in 1974, and in July 2020 [[Emmanuel Macron|President Emmanuel Macron]] reverted to the darker navy blue at the Élysée Palace, as a symbol of the French Revolution.

National flag, a horizontal tricolor of black, red and gold bands. Black-red-gold appeared in 1848 in the [[German Confederation]], and the [[German Empire]] also used it from 1848 to 1849. It was adopted for the [[Weimar Republic]] from 1919 to 1933, was also used by the German Democratic Republic (1949–1990), and was restored for the Federal Republic in 1949. A competing black-white-red tradition, used by the German Empire until 1918–19, was revived by the Nazis in 1933 along with the [[Swastika]] flag. Black-red-gold is an official symbol protected against defamation, punishable by a fine or imprisonment up to three years.

National flag, colloquially called the Tiranga, a horizontal tricolor of saffron, white and green with a navy blue 24-spoke Ashoka Chakra at its center. It was adopted in its present form by the Constituent Assembly on July 22, 1947. It is based on the Swaraj flag of the [[Indian National Congress]], which [[Mahatma Gandhi]] adapted from a design by Pingali Venkayya. [[Jawaharlal Nehru]] replaced its charkha with the chakra in 1947. A 2002 Supreme Court directive, on an appeal by a private citizen, led to amendments allowing private use.

National flag, a white banner with a red disc at its center. Officially called the *Nisshōki* (flag of the sun) and popularly the *Hinomaru*, it was designated by the Act on National Flag and Anthem in 1999. Two 1870 proclamations made a sun disc flag the national flag for merchant ships and the navy. The sun is central to Japanese mythology, as the emperor is said to descend directly from the [[Shinto]] sun goddess [[Amaterasu]]. The flag became a major symbol of the [[Empire of Japan]] during the [[Meiji Restoration]], and it remained contentious in public schools after [[World War II]].

National flag, a vertical tricolor of green, white and red with the national coat of arms at the center of the white stripe. The colors were adopted after independence from [[Spain]] during the [[Mexican War of Independence]]. Agustín de Iturbide decreed the national flag in November 1821, and it was first officially used in July 1822. The coat of arms is based on the Aztec symbol for [[Tenochtitlan]], now [[Mexico City]], and recalls a legend of a golden eagle sitting on a [[Cactus|nopal cactus]] while devouring a serpent. The legend signaled where the Aztecs were to found their city.

National flag, a tricolor of three equal horizontal bands: white, blue and red. Accounts link its origin to the tricolor of the Dutch Republic. [[Peter the Great]] first introduced the design in 1693, and in 1705 it was adopted as the civil ensign of the [[Tsardom of Russia]]. In 1896, [[Nicholas II]] replaced the black-yellow-white national flag with the white-blue-red tricolor. The [[Bolsheviks]] banned it after the [[October Revolution]] of 1917, though the White movement flew it in the [[Russian Civil War]]. It was readopted in August 1991, and [[Boris Yeltsin]] specified its current proportions and shades in 1993.

National flag of the [[United States]], with 13 horizontal stripes alternating red and white and a blue canton bearing 50 white five-pointed stars. The stripes represent the original British colonies that won independence in the [[American Revolutionary War]], and the stars represent the states. The flag evolved gradually and was not designed by any one person. The first official flag resembling it, used from 1775 to 1777, had the [[Union Jack]] in its canton. The flag came to symbolize the Union in the [[American Civil War]]. The 50-star design was ordered by [[Dwight D. Eisenhower|President Eisenhower]] in 1959 and adopted in July 1960, after Hawaii's admission.
